extracted.intended_audience: students or self-learners studying elementary/arithmetic fraction operations
extracted.subtask_description: Step-by-step procedural rules and recommended algorithms for performing addition, subtraction, multiplication and division of fractions (often presented with tabular/row layouts and multiple alternative methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication of fractions (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiply one fraction by another by combining their parts; the product is obtained by multiplying the respective numbers composing the fractions (numerators with numerators and denominators with denominators) using arranged rows or copied lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents several equivalent practical methods: place fractions in rows, copy appropriate rows and multiply corresponding entries to form a new row that contains the product. Several worked ways are given (copying rows, multiplying line-by-line, or by grouping). Advice: arrange numbers on lines to avoid error and to make the operation clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplying fractions by whole numbers / mixed numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: To multiply a fraction by a whole number (or vice versa), treat the whole number as a fraction (or decompose it into units) and perform multiplication as between fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods include reducing the whole to units or placing the whole's value in a row with denominator 1, or splitting the whole into parts and multiplying each part by the fraction then summing. Examples and several sequences show converting wholes to like units before multiplying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiply many fractions / sequential multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiplying several fractions together, perform the multiplications sequentially or combine numerators and denominators across all factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer cancelling common factors between any numerator and any denominator before performing full multiplications to avoid large intermediate numbers. The book illustrates doing multiplications in rows and cancelling across rows to simplify computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding a common denominator for addition
rubrics_metrics.description: To add fractions reduce them to a common denominator (make denominators equal) before summing numerators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text describes multiple ways to get a common denominator: multiply all denominators together, use cross-multiplication (incrociando), or find suitable partitions so denominators coincide. Several step-by-step row/table methods are recommended to align parts and then sum the corresponding numerators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition by partitioning and aligning (row/table methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative to raw common-denominator computation is to partition fractions into like parts and arrange them in rows so like parts can be summed directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tables or lines where each fraction's parts occupy corresponding columns/rows; copy rows as needed so that units match, then add vertically. The manual emphasizes that arranging the data in a table reduces tedium and error for many numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtraction of fractions (reduce to common unit and handle remainders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtract fractions by bringing them to the same denomination/unit and subtracting numerators; when a remainder requires borrowing, convert to smaller units (fractions of the unit) to continue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses methods for borrowing/transforming units so subtraction can proceed (e.g., converting one unit into multiple smaller parts). Several worked examples show converting a remainder into appropriate fractional units and continuing the subtraction until the remainder is resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of fractions (invert-and-multiply principle and variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: To divide by a fraction, invert (take reciprocal of) the divisor and multiply; different procedures are given depending on which terms are whole or fractional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise presents many cases (fraction ÷ fraction, whole ÷ fraction, fraction ÷ whole, mixed situations) and prescribes reducing cases to multiplication by reciprocals or arranging terms in tables. It also discusses successive partitioning and use of tables to find quotients and remainders in division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction / simplification to lowest terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Always reduce fractions by cancelling common factors either before performing operations (recommended) or after, to simplify computation and final results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice includes canceling factors between numerators and denominators across multiplied factors, reducing intermediate results to avoid large numbers, and dividing out common divisors at convenient stages. The text warns that not reducing produces unnecessary labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose method to minimize labor / avoid tedium
rubrics_metrics.description: Select among the multiple presented algorithms (cross-multiplication, common-denominator by LCM, partitioning, table/row copying) the one that makes the arithmetic least burdensome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly recommends the method that leads to fewer and smaller intermediate computations. For long or many-term operations, using tabular arrangement and cancellation is preferred to repeated heavy arithmetic; avoid unnecessarily creating very large denominators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tables and copying rows to organize work
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize fractions and intermediate quantities in tables or rows (tauole, righe) and copy rows as needed to perform operations systematically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables reduce error and tedium, allow easy visual alignment of like parts, and facilitate repeated operations (e.g., multiplying a row by several numbers). The text gives examples of constructing tables up to large counts (noting ability to work up to 1000) and copying rows to produce products or sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling remainders and iterative decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: When operations produce remainders (especially in division and subtraction), repeatedly decompose the remainder into smaller fractional units and continue the operation until a suitable unit is obtained or the remainder vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual describes successive decomposition (taking the remainder, writing it as parts of the next smaller unit, dividing those, etc.) with multiple examples showing repeated steps until the desired quotient or exact subtraction is achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross methods ('incrociando') for generating common denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific technique described uses cross-multiplication of rows ('incrociando') to produce a common denominator and thereby enable addition or comparison of fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The procedure: cross-multiply numerators and denominators as prescribed to generate a common basis, then sum the resulting numerators. The text shows this as one of several equivalent approaches and suggests choosing it when convenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert between fraction types and reduce to a common nature
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining fractions of different 'nature' (different denominators or mixed compositions), transform them to a single chosen nature/unit so operations become uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include converting all parts to a particular denominator and then operating; the text emphasizes that making all fractions the same 'nature' (unit) simplifies addition, subtraction, and comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary splitting; prefer grouping similar parts
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, group like fractional parts together rather than repeatedly splitting units, to make addition/multiplication easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts many equivalent methods and recommends grouping and working with common parts where it reduces the number of operations, giving advice to avoid excessively fragmenting units unless needed for exactness.
